title: Pride and Prejudice - Chapter III
author: Jane Austen
description: The Meryton Assembly introduces the primary conflict and characters of the novel. Mr. Bingley is universally loved for his amiability, while Mr. Darcy is universally loathed for his pride, specifically after slighting Elizabeth Bennet.
historical_context: The public assembly was a vital social hub in Regency England, allowing for supervised interaction between the gentry and local families. Social standing was determined within minutes by a combination of income and perceived manners.

analysis.insight: Darcy's reputation is built in 'five minutes' based on his income, then destroyed in 'half the evening' based on his manners. This rapid social tallying shows the high-pressure environment of the Regency assembly.
analysis.anchor_text: report, which was in general circulation within five minutes after his entrance, of his having ten thousand a year

analysis.insight: Bingley and Darcy serve as foils. Bingley is 'easy, unaffected' and 'unreserved,' whereas Darcy is 'proud' and 'above his company.' Austen uses their differing reactions to the same room to define their characters.
analysis.anchor_text: Mr. Bingley had soon made himself acquainted with all the principal people in the room

analysis.insight: Mrs. Bennet's 'particular resentment' against Darcy is rooted not just in his rudeness, but in the fact that he represents a closed door for her daughters' social advancement.
analysis.anchor_text: dislike of his general behaviour was sharpened into particular resentment by his having slighted one of her daughters

analysis.insight: Elizabeth’s decision to tell the story of her own slight with 'great spirit' establishes her as a woman who uses wit as a shield against social humiliation.
analysis.anchor_text: lively, playful disposition, which delighted in anything ridiculous

analysis.insight: Mrs. Bennet’s report on who Bingley danced with twice highlights the competitive nature of the marriage market, where 'beauty' is a quantifiable asset.
analysis.anchor_text: he actually danced with her twice; and she was the only creature in the room that he asked a second time

analysis.insight: Mr. Bennet’s hope that his wife’s views would be 'disappointed' shows his desire for peace over his family's social success, further illustrating the disconnect in their marriage.

analysis.insight: Darcy's behavior—spending the evening 'walking about the room, speaking occasionally to one of his own party'—is a performance of social superiority that the local gentry correctly identifies as 'proud.'
analysis.anchor_text: spent the rest of the evening in walking about the room, speaking occasionally to one of his own party

footnotes_and_analyses.title: The Economy of 'Ten Thousand'
footnotes_and_analyses.content: Darcy's wealth (10,000 pounds a year) would make him one of the wealthiest men in England, far exceeding Bingley's 5,000. In Regency terms, this is not just 'rich'; it is 'magnate' territory. His refusal to dance with local women is not just a personal slight, but a statement on the vast economic gulf between the high aristocracy and the rural gentry.

footnotes_and_analyses.title: The First Overheard Dialogue
footnotes_and_analyses.content: Austen's use of eavesdropping as a plot device begins here. Elizabeth's character is defined not by her own words, but by her reaction to Darcy's words. By laughing at his rudeness, she claims an intellectual superiority that Darcy—at this stage—cannot see. This is the seed of the 'Prejudice' mentioned in the title.

summary: Chapter 3 introduces the Meryton ball, the charm of Mr. Bingley, and the infamous pride of Mr. Darcy, whose slight against Elizabeth Bennet sets the stage for the novel's central conflict.
